S06-R001-P002.en: Presenter, seminar participants, audience, supervising teacher. [1] Seminar process and results — Explain what you presented at the seminar, especially material not included in the presentation slides. Describe the questions, answers and discussion. 1.1 Problem and overview. Google Trends data show that searches for ESG, CSR and sustainability rose sharply at two turning points, in 2021 and 2025. In 2021, the inauguration of the Biden administration coincided with BlackRock's requirement for ESG investment; in 2025, the emergence of high-performance AI and geopolitical instability again prompted discussion of the conditions for corporate survival. Both turning points reveal a shared pattern: the greater the external shock, the more the discussion of corporate sustainability resurfaces. Yet there has been insufficient examination of whether ESG and CSR actually provide a framework for responding to such shocks.

S06-R001-P003.en: With this problem in mind, I used Peter Thiel's Zero to One as the theoretical foundation. Thiel, who studied philosophy and law at Stanford and co-founded PayPal and Palantir, centers his argument on the counterintuitive claim that competition destroys value. In perfect competition, ATC = MC = MR and profits converge to zero, leaving firms to focus on survival itself. A monopoly, by contrast, can use stable excess profits to support long-term thinking, R&D, better employee treatment and tangible social contributions. Two hypotheses follow. A) There is almost no correlation between social responsibility or giving back and sustainability. B) Good monopolies can respond to rapid change.

S06-R001-P004.en: 1.2 Data analysis. I divided the sample into two groups. Group A consisted of ten innovative monopoly companies mentioned directly by Peter Thiel. Group B consisted of large companies that actively implemented ESG after 2021. I collected four years of data for each group. The evaluation measures were the Rule of 40 (revenue growth rate + operating margin), ROIC, FCF margin, R&D expenditure ratio and ESG score. The methods were Spearman correlation analysis, SHAP machine-learning factor analysis and TensorFlow counterfactual analysis. I introduced counterfactual analysis to simulate how performance would change if ESG were removed.

S06-R002-P001.en: To establish data reliability, I collected the data statically in v1 and then recollected them dynamically through the Yahoo Finance Query API in v2.5, comparing the two versions for validation. ESG scores came from external rating agencies. Revenue growth and operating margin for the Rule of 40 were calculated from annual financial statements. The entire process was implemented in Python, using an XGBoost model and the SHAP library to quantify each variable's contribution to the Rule of 40.

S06-R002-P003.en: Spearman correlation analysis found correlations with ESG scores of −0.17 for the Rule of 40, 0.10 for ROIC, 0.02 for FCF margin and −0.52 for the R&D expenditure ratio. The −0.52 correlation with the R&D ratio indicates that higher ESG scores operate in a direction that suppresses innovation investment. In the SHAP analysis, the ESG score's feature importance was 0.05 or less and was not statistically significant as a determinant of the Rule of 40. FCF margin, the R&D ratio and ROIC, by contrast, ranked as the top three determinants.

S06-R003-P001.en: In the group comparison, Group B's ESG scores exceeded 70, well above Group A's scores in the 50s, yet both its Rule of 40 and ROIC were substantially lower than Group A's. TensorFlow counterfactual analysis showed a small increase in the Rule of 40 when ESG was removed. This points in the opposite direction from the conventional belief that ESG improves corporate performance. Both hypotheses were supported by the data. I concluded the presentation by arguing that the substantive drivers of sustainability lie in a monopoly strategy based on technological advantage and philosophical identity, rather than spending on social responsibility.

S06-R004-P001.en: Three questions were raised. The first concerned the self-corrosion of monopoly: if external competitive pressure disappears, might the motivation to innovate internally weaken? I first noted that Thiel himself acknowledged this limitation to some extent. However, firms possessing both a strong philosophical identity and technological advantage do not simply remain satisfied with the present. They continually redefine their direction on the basis of that identity. I answered that companies in which these two elements reinforce one another meet the conditions for a ‘good monopoly.’

S06-R004-P002.en: The second question was whether advocating monopoly at the level of national institutions could be an extreme position. I proposed three concrete mechanisms: allow technological monopoly while strictly applying existing competition law to pricing and restrictions on market entry; require a technology-disclosure roadmap or an R&D reinvestment ratio as a condition of state support; and redesign antitrust review around contributions to innovation rather than revenue. I explained that the presentation's central claim was that supporting technological monopoly is more effective than mandatory ESG for both national industrial competitiveness and corporate sustainability. Consumer protection should be discussed alongside this as a separate matter of institutional design.

S06-R004-P003.en: The third question concerned methodology: can Groups A and B be directly compared when they differ in corporate life cycle and industry, and were the data aligned to the same period after each company's establishment? I acknowledged that this analysis did not compare identical numbers of years after IPO. However, the companies selected for Group A had already established market dominance, so the concentration of R&D spending in the early life cycle can be regarded as controlled to some extent within the four-year period. More fundamentally, the purpose was not to compare identical periods measured from incorporation, but to examine which corporate identities were structurally advantaged under the same macroeconomic shocks in 2025–2026. I therefore explained that the focus was on sharing the same environment rather than the same corporate age. Reanalysis using identical post-IPO years and additional controls for industrial sector remain future tasks. [2] Feedback and collaboration — Describe feedback from teammates, the audience, the supervising teacher or yourself. Describe any specific efforts to collaborate with teammates throughout the seminar. Feedback from the supervising teacher.

S06-R004-P004.en: 1. Operational definition of sustainability. The most substantial feedback, and also the most controversial question, concerned the operational definition of sustainability itself. The teacher's initial confusion was whether sustainability referred to society or to the company itself. The teacher asked whether technological monopoly affects society's sustainability. To be clear, I meant corporate sustainability. The topic concerned how firms should respond to accelerating changes in social structures, as in the familiar idea of a company lasting a century. It focused on the essential nature of firms as profit-seeking organizations and asked how companies can endure.

S06-R004-P005.en: 2. Discussion of a conflict with another team member's argument. A disagreement with the teacher arose because my argument appeared to conflict with that of another team member working on the same topic, monopoly, and using the same book. The teacher asked whether Red Bull's monopoly strategy—supporting sports teams, supporting less mainstream sports such as extreme sports, and establishing an identity—was actually closer to ESG, and said it was difficult to understand my conclusion that ESG contributes little to sustainability. I believe this conflict arose because two definitions had become ambiguous. 2-1. Definition of monopoly and technological monopoly. Both this report and the seminar focus on the good monopoly discussed by Thiel. A high market share alone does not constitute monopoly, and it should not be confused with oligopoly. Thiel's monopoly has four elements: network effects, economies of scale, identity (which I additionally define as philosophical identity) and technology (which I additionally define as overwhelming technological capability). Fundamentally, all four conditions must be met.

S06-R004-P006.en: Red Bull, which the teacher described as ESG, operates in a highly inelastic beverage industry with little fluctuation, already meeting the conditions of network effects and economies of scale. It has established an identity extending beyond beverages into extreme sports. The presenter who focused on Red Bull simply did not clearly explain its technological breakthroughs. Red Bull is also attempting monopolization in technology, for example by collaborating with Ball Corporation, a can manufacturer, and the filling specialist Rauch to build an integrated smart factory using pure aluminum cans. In other words, it is already a monopoly to some extent, while ESG has emerged as an additional effect of its monopoly strategy. This does not change my earlier argument that technological monopoly is a superior strategy to ESG.

S06-R005-P002.en: It is true that the other presenter provided an insufficient explanation of the technological aspects, and I acknowledge that social contributions made during identity formation gave the teacher considerable grounds for confusion. However, this alone is difficult to regard as contradicting the superiority of technological monopoly. As I explained in the seminar, Red Bull's current stagnation and the emergence of the powerful competitor Monster can also be seen as examples of Red Bull not yet demonstrating a clear technological monopoly. To take an extreme example, if Red Bull had an overwhelming technological monopoly in can manufacturing, it might have achieved a far higher market share and a stronger advantage despite Monster—a competitor combining diverse flavors with a strategy of following Red Bull as a substitute—through dramatically reduced manufacturing costs and value for money.

S06-R005-P003.en: To summarize my argument, I agree that my analysis centered on monopoly, particularly technological monopoly, can appear to conflict with the other member's presentation on Red Bull. Red Bull's strategy in particular may be regarded as closer to ESG. However:

S06-R005-P004.en: 1. Red Bull is a company somewhat removed from technological monopoly (the beverage market is inelastic and does not fluctuate greatly).

S06-R005-P005.en: 2. Red Bull's strategy also fits the monopoly described by Peter Thiel (identity).

S06-R005-P006.en: 3. Red Bull is also pursuing a technological-monopoly strategy.

S06-R005-P007.en: 4. In my view, if Red Bull had pursued technological acquisition more aggressively, it might not have remained in its present stagnation. These points summarize my position. In conclusion, the arguments may appear opposed, as the supervising teacher suggested, but this judgment rests on a highly limited understanding of the content and examples. I believe there was room for misunderstanding or a communication problem during the seminar.

S06-R005-P008.en: 2-2. Misunderstandings about sustainability and ESG. I believe the definitions of sustainability and ESG also need to be clarified. As stated earlier, I operationally defined sustainability as corporate sustainability, and ESG likewise referred to ESG management or strategy. This was the starting point of the research question and ultimately led to a conclusion about the effectiveness of ESG management.

S06-R005-P009.en: Corporate sustainability is very difficult to define in practice, and it is absolutely impossible to predict the future accurately. I therefore chose to investigate it through indicators such as the Rule of 40, ROIC and FCF. The analysis found that companies using ESG management as their principal strategy, represented by high ESG scores, did not have a major influence on those indicators, and no correlation with ESG score was found.

S06-R005-P010.en: However, treating this as meaning that ESG is meaningless or useless would be a generalization. My intended comparison with ESG was that technological-monopoly strategy contributes more to actual corporate sustainability, and that this analysis therefore made it difficult to identify a correlation with ESG score. I agree that ESG has been used and adopted because it is a method whose significance has been demonstrated to some extent. Yet my own research did not produce that result, and I believe this allows an answer to the question of whether ESG management is meaningless.

S06-R005-P011.en: Ultimately, ESG simply did not correspond to the sustainability measures I specified. I believe it is a logical error to turn this into a conclusion that ESG is ultimately meaningless.

S06-R006-P001.en: [3] Reflections and further inquiry — Describe your reflections on the seminar research and presentation, focusing on the feedback. Describe any additional research after the seminar. Questions raised by the supervising teacher's feedback.

S06-R006-P002.en: 1. Is ESG management a successful management strategy? The central issue in the teacher's feedback was a challenge to my assessment of ESG management's effectiveness. When I presented the finding that correlations between ESG score and the Rule of 40, ROIC and FCF margin were not significant, the teacher asked why I regarded ESG as ineffective when it had been adopted as a strategy whose effectiveness had been established. What needs clarification is that the absence of ESG effectiveness in this analysis is a finding within the corporate-sustainability indicators I operationally defined. Whether ESG management has meaningful social and environmental effects and whether it drives a firm's financial sustainability are separate questions. This research sought to answer the latter. Within that scope, ESG score had an importance of 0.05 or less as a determinant of the Rule of 40. Concluding that all ESG management is meaningless would be a logical leap. My claim was that technological monopoly is more effective than ESG management as a strategic option for corporate sustainability.

S06-R006-P003.en: 2. Moral superiority. A recurring pattern in the teacher's feedback throughout the seminar was the presupposition that a critical conclusion about ESG management was morally problematic. Although I explicitly stated, while discussing greenwashing and limitations to ESG's effectiveness, that this did not deny ESG's social significance itself, counterexamples continued to be raised. Questions such as whether monopoly companies benefit society and what happens to social responsibility if ESG is abandoned ultimately arose, I believe, from viewing the presentation through a moral framework about firms' social roles. Yet the starting point was structure, not morality. I analyzed the strategies through which companies, as profit-seeking organizations, survive rapid environmental change. If it is logically possible for monopolies to use stable excess profits for R&D and tangible social contributions, the premise that technological monopoly is a morally inferior choice does not hold. I also noted that a monopoly's advantages and freedom of choice can create room for a company to spend on giving back and welfare.

S06-R006-P004.en: I agree that questioning the effectiveness of ESG management may provoke resistance grounded in an unconscious sense of social or moral superiority. But firms are fundamentally profit-seeking organizations, and being a monopoly may allow them to generate profits for a long period and use those profits to realize social distribution and justice. A rebuttal based on moral superiority is therefore unlikely to directly refute this presentation's argument. It is structurally impossible for a company whose profits converge to zero under perfect competition to fulfill its social responsibilities. A company with monopoly excess profits instead has the material foundation to sustain R&D, employee welfare and social contributions over the long term. Between compulsory ESG that appears morally correct and a monopoly-profit structure that makes actual social contributions possible, this presentation maintains that the latter is more effective.

S06-R006-P005.en: 3. Genuine socially responsible management. Taken together, the conflict over Red Bull and the operational definition of sustainability suggest that most of the teacher's counterexamples arose from conflating technological monopoly, ESG and social responsibility. The suggestion that Red Bull's extreme-sports identity strategy is close to ESG is a misunderstanding caused by treating philosophical identity, one of the four elements of monopoly defined by Thiel, as equivalent to social contributions. Red Bull's sports sponsorship emerged as a by-product of a monopoly strategy for building brand identity, and it is difficult to regard this as structurally identical to ESG management. More importantly, when discussing genuine socially responsible management, there is a paradox: a stable structure of excess profits through technological monopoly may enable longer-term and more tangible contributions than compulsory ESG spending. The position maintained throughout the presentation was that Palantir's technological support for the security of Western allies and its continuing reinvestment in R&D may constitute a more fundamental approach to both corporate sustainability and social contributions than compulsory spending intended to raise ESG scores.
